interest: This file provides a valuable window into U.S.-Japan cultural diplomacy and archival recovery in the aftermath of the catastrophic 1923 Great Kanto Earthquake, which destroyed the Tokyo Imperial University Library and Japan's original treaty copies. It reveals how the U.S. State Department utilized historical treaty reproductions—and remarkably, an original quintuplicate copy of the 1857 Shimoda Convention—as instruments of goodwill to reaffirm bilateral friendship at a time of rising Pacific tensions. Ambassador Castle's address is especially noteworthy for historians, as it contrasts Townsend Harris's 1858 clause pledging American mediation with 1930s U.S. Senate isolationism, while the second exchange illustrates how American missionary educators, such as Frank Cary in Otaru, integrated founding diplomatic artifacts into regional educational curricula.
overview: This file (State Department decimal 894.414) covers diplomatic correspondence and press reports from April to June 1930 concerning the supply and presentation of historical U.S.-Japan treaty documents to replace originals destroyed in the Tokyo fire of 1923. U.S. Ambassador William R. Castle, Jr. reports on an April 14, 1930 ceremony at the newly reconstructed Tokyo Imperial University Library, where he formally presented photostatic copies of the 1854 Treaty of Kanagawa and the 1858 Harris Treaty, along with an original quintuplicate copy of the 1857 Shimoda Convention, to University President Kiheiji Onozuka in the presence of Japanese dignitaries such as Vice-Minister Shigeru Yoshida. An accompanying clipping from The Japan Advertiser details the speeches highlighting Townsend Harris's diplomacy, Emperor Meiji's reforms, and John D. Rockefeller, Jr.'s contribution to rebuilding the library. Later correspondence in May and June 1930 documents Ambassador Castle's request on behalf of Reverend Frank Cary of the Japan Kumiai Christian Church for photostatic copies of the signature pages of the 1854 and 1858 treaties for educational use in schools in Otaru, which the State Department subsequently furnished to Chargé d'Affaires Edwin L. Neville.

subfiles.about: Ambassador Castle reports on the presentation of photostatic and original early treaty documents to the President of Tokyo Imperial University.
subfiles.from: William R. Castle, Jr., U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Ambassador William R. Castle, Jr. informs the Secretary of State that on April 14, 1930, he presented photostatic copies of the Treaties of 1854 and 1858 and an original quintuplicate copy of the 1857 treaty to President Kiheiji Onozuka of Tokyo Imperial University. The formal presentation took place in the assembly room of the university's new library before approximately seventy-five guests, including Vice-Minister for Foreign Affairs Shigeru Yoshida and Dr. Samuel McCune Lindsay. Castle notes that the Japanese press covered the event extensively and that the American gift created a highly favorable public impression.
subfiles.title: Despatch from Ambassador Castle on Presentation of Historic Treaties to Tokyo Imperial University
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, U.S. Secretary of State

subfiles.about: A newspaper report detailing the presentation ceremony at Tokyo Imperial University Library and transcribing addresses by Ambassador Castle and President Onozuka.
subfiles.summary: A newspaper article from The Japan Advertiser describing the April 14, 1930 ceremony where Ambassador Castle delivered reproductions of early treaties to Tokyo Imperial University to replace documents lost in the 1923 fire. The article transcribes Castle's address discussing the terms of Townsend Harris's 1858 treaty, its surprising mediation clause, and Emperor Meiji's leadership in modernizing Japan. It also quotes University President Onozuka's response thanking the American government, noting the documents will aid the Historiographic Institute, and acknowledging John D. Rockefeller, Jr.'s funding for the library's reconstruction.
subfiles.title: Newspaper Clipping from The Japan Advertiser on Presentation of Treaties

subfiles.about: Ambassador Castle requests twelve photostats of the signature pages of the 1854 and 1858 treaties for educational use in church schools in Otaru.
subfiles.from: William R. Castle, Jr., U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Castle requests that the State Department supply the Embassy with six photostatic copies of the signature page of the 1854 Treaty of Peace, Amity and Commerce and six copies of the final page of the 1858 Harris Treaty. The request is made on behalf of Reverend Frank Cary, Chairman of the Japan Kumiai Christian Church, for educational use in his schools in Otaru, Japan. Castle notes that Cary has volunteered to pay all costs incurred in preparing the reproductions.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 137 from Ambassador Castle Requesting Treaty Photostats for Frank Cary
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, U.S. Secretary of State

subfiles.about: The Department of State transmits requested photostats of the signature pages of the 1854 and 1858 treaties for delivery to Frank Cary in Otaru.
subfiles.summary: The Department of State acknowledges receipt of Embassy Despatch No. 137 and transmits the requested enclosures to American Chargé d'Affaires ad interim Edwin L. Neville in Tokyo. The enclosures comprise six photostat copies of the final signature page of the 1854 Treaty of Peace, Amity, and Commerce and six copies of the final page of the 1858 Harris Treaty. These copies are forwarded for delivery to Frank Cary, Chairman of the Japan Kumiai Christian Church, for use in his schools in Otaru.
subfiles.title: Instruction No. 72 from Department of State Transmitting Treaty Photostats
subfiles.to: Edwin L. Neville, U.S. Chargé d'Affaires ad interim, Tokyo
